I'm 62 years old, and I've been farming these 16.1 mu in Quzhou County for 40 years. I studied agricultural science, so I understand the theory, but four decades of walking these fields has taught me that theory only gets you so far—you have to know your own soil, your own well, and your own limitations. It's just my wife and me now, so labor is my tightest constraint. I split the land into 10 mu of wheat-maize double crop and 6.1 mu of cotton. That gives me grain for security and cotton for cash, which is insurance I learned to value after a bad drought in the late 1990s.

The wheat I sowed last October is at jointing now. I applied a base dressing of compound fertilizer at sowing, and the stand is uniform, but the lower leaves are showing slight yellowing—classic N deficiency at this stage. I'm targeting 480 kg/mu, so I'm applying a urea topdress at jointing delivering about 12 kg N/mu, followed immediately by irrigation to move it into the root zone. I'll irrigate twice more if needed: once at booting and once at grain filling. May has been trending dry in recent years, and I'd rather waste a bit on pumping costs than lose yield. I'm also spraying a fungicide this week to stay ahead of powdery mildew.

For maize, the critical factor is the turnaround window. After wheat harvest in early June, I have maybe five days to get the maize in the ground before I lose yield potential. I'm using a hybrid variety—probably Zhengdan 958—and band-applying compound fertilizer at planting. I'm targeting 520 kg/mu, so my total N budget is 18 kg/mu, split between the base and a urea side-dress at V8. Summer rainfall should handle most of it, but I'll irrigate at tasseling and again at grain filling if the soil moisture drops.

Cotton is my cash crop but it's labor-hungry. I'm planting Bt cotton in mid-April with plastic mulch to warm the soil and suppress early weeds. I'm budgeting 15 kg N/mu across three applications: base at planting, then topdresses at flowering and boll-setting. I'll irrigate twice—flowering and boll-setting are non-negotiable. With good management and decent weather, I expect around 280 kg/mu of seed cotton. But picking will require hired labor; my wife and I can't handle 6 mu of cotton alone in October.

My total cash outlay for inputs and hired labor this season will be about 10,000 yuan. That's a significant share of our savings, but I've learned the hard way that skimping on fertilizer or irrigation to save a few hundred yuan can cost you thousands in lost yield. I sleep better knowing I gave the crop what it needed.
